newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS-EU merger panel against Cablevision deal-sources.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-EU merger panel against Cablevision deal-sources.

text.p: A European Union merger panel advised the European Commission on Monday to ban the cable television venture between Spanish telecoms group Telefonica de Espana and pay TV giant Sogecable SA, EU sources said.
The Commission usually follows the view of the committee and unless the companies withdraw their notification, the European Union executive looks set to decide to block the deal later this month.
"The discussion at the committee showed that everybody except Spain was of the opinion that the proposal on the table is unacceptable," one source said.
The members of the committee believed the venture would lead to a dominant position on the market, hurting competition.
Earlier, the sources said Telefonica was set to pull out of the deal because of expected Commission opposition.
The partly state-owned Spanish telecoms operator had indicated it preferred to drop out now rather than face a likely ruling against the venture by the EU executive.

But it might face resistance from Sogecable SA, a unit of Promotora de Informaciones SA and France's Canal Plus, which does not appear willing to let the deal die without receiving compensation, sources said.
"Telefonica has indicated that it is ready to withdraw from the deal...but it appears that Sogecable and probably Canal Plus France are not ready to give up," one source said.
The sources said the Commission may fine the companies for going ahead with the Cablevision deal last year without seeking prior Commission clearance.
The joint venture was set up by Telefonica and Sogecable SA in July 1995 to operate and distribute pay television and multimedia in Spain via cable TV networks.
Sogecable and Canal Plus Espana, a subsidiary of the French company, are both in the fast-growing pay-television business and Telefonica is the country's dominant telecoms operator.
Ten million households have televisions in Spain but only 200,000 have access to cable, making it one of the largest untapped markets left in western Europe.
Company sources told daily El Mundo last week Telefonica's directors would recommend the dissolution of Cablevision at the next board meeting on November 11.
When it began a full probe into the case in July, the Commission expressed strong doubts about it because Telefonica still has a monopoly on the local telecommunications market.
The operation would affect the market for cable television services and would also have an indirect impact on the telephone and data transmission sectors, it said at the time.
The Commission, which vets all major corporate agreements which affect trade in the EU, has become increasingly tough on media alliances and especially on cable pay-television deals.
